items.prompt: Choose the relative pronoun. The girl ___ won the race is my cousin.

options.text: which
options.why: Which is used for things and animals, not people.

options.text: where
who
whose
options.why: Whose shows that something belongs to someone.

hints: The missing word adds information about the girl.
Think about which relative pronoun is used for people.
Ask: is the girl a person, a thing or a place?
items.explanation: Who is used for people. The clause who won the race tells us which girl.

items.prompt: Write who or which. The bicycle ___ I borrowed has a flat tyre.
hints: The missing word adds information about the bicycle.
Who is for people. Think about the word that is used for things.
Ask: is a bicycle a person or a thing?
items.explanation: Which is used for things, so the bicycle which I borrowed is correct. That would also work here.

items.prompt: Which sentence contains a relative clause?

options.text: The dog barks at night.
options.why: This is a simple sentence with one clause.

options.text: The dog that lives next door barks at night.
When the dog barks, I wake up.
options.why: When the dog barks tells us when something happens. It does not add information about a noun.

options.text: The dog barks because it is lonely.
options.why: Because it is lonely gives a reason. It is not a relative clause.

hints: A relative clause adds information about a noun.
Look for who, which, that, whose or where straight after a noun.
Find the word dog in each sentence. What comes straight after it?
items.explanation: That lives next door tells us more about the dog, so it is a relative clause.

items.prompt: Match each beginning to the best ending.
pairs: who helped me with my project.
hints: Each ending starts with a different relative pronoun.
Where goes with places, when with times, who with people and which with things. Whose shows belonging.
Start with the day. Which ending begins with a time word?
items.explanation: Where follows a place (the house), when follows a time (the day), who follows a person (the teacher) and which follows a thing (the book). Whose shows the song belongs to the singer.

items.prompt: Sort the phrases by the relative pronoun that fits the gap.
hints: Look at the noun before each gap.
Ask: is it a person, a thing or a place?
Start with the baker. Is a baker a person, a thing or a place?
items.explanation: People take who (the baker, the pilot), things take which (the umbrella, the song) and places take where (the market, the island).

items.prompt: Join the sentences using whose. I met a boy. His father is a pilot.

answers: I met a boy whose father is a pilot
I met a boy, whose father is a pilot

hints: Whose shows that something belongs to someone.
Whose replaces his, so you do not need his any more.
Find the word in the second sentence that whose will replace.
items.explanation: Whose replaces his and joins the sentences: I met a boy whose father is a pilot.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly around the extra information?

options.text: My aunt who lives, in Surabaya is visiting us.
options.why: The commas must go around the whole clause who lives in Surabaya.

options.text: My aunt, who lives in Surabaya is visiting us.
options.why: The extra information needs a comma at the end as well as the start.

options.text: My, aunt who lives in Surabaya, is visiting us.
options.why: The first comma should come after aunt, not after my.

options.text: My aunt, who lives in Surabaya, is visiting us.

hints: Find the extra information first.
Extra information is separated by a comma before it and a comma after it.
Underline who lives in Surabaya in your head. Where should the commas go?
items.explanation: The clause who lives in Surabaya adds extra information about my aunt, so it needs a comma before it and a comma after it.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a relative pronoun incorrectly?

options.text: The cat which lives next door is very fluffy.
options.why: This is correct. Which can be used for animals.

options.text: The man which fixed our roof was friendly.
The town where I was born is by the sea.
options.why: This is correct. Where is used for places.

options.text: The girl whose bag was lost found it later.
options.why: This is correct. Whose shows the bag belongs to the girl.

hints: Check each relative pronoun against the noun in front of it.
Remember: who for people, which for things and animals, where for places, whose for belonging.
Start with the man. Which pronoun should be used for a person?
items.explanation: A man is a person, so the sentence should say the man who fixed our roof. Which is for things and animals.

items.prompt: Write the missing relative pronoun. Komodo Island, ___ is in Indonesia, is home to the largest lizard in the world.
hints: The missing word adds extra information about a place.
The clause is between commas, so that cannot be used here.
Ask: is Komodo Island a person or a thing? Then choose the pronoun.
items.explanation: The extra information is about an island, so which is used. That cannot start a clause between commas.

items.prompt: Read: The pupils who finished early read quietly. What does this sentence tell us?

options.text: Only some pupils finished early, and those pupils read quietly.
All the pupils finished early.
options.why: Without commas, the clause picks out some pupils, not all of them.

options.text: The pupils read quietly because the teacher asked them to.
options.why: The sentence does not give a reason.

options.text: The pupils finished reading early.
options.why: Finished early is about their work, and reading came afterwards.

hints: Notice that there are no commas around who finished early.
A clause without commas tells us which ones we are talking about.
Ask: does the sentence mean every pupil, or only certain pupils?
items.explanation: Without commas, who finished early tells us which pupils read quietly: only the ones who finished early. With commas, it would mean all the pupils finished early.
